_meta.token_syntax: {{slope=<fraction rise/run, e.g. 1/12>|<source-stated text>}} and {{len=<millimetres>|<source-stated text>}} are converted by the page's unit selector.
_meta.tagline: How steep a ramp may be, and how far it can run before a rest. Most codes cap the slope at {{slope=1/12|1:12}}; the Guidebook position is {{slope=1/20|1:20}}.
_meta.best_practice_basis: Best practice is what benefits the people it is for most. For ramp gradient, a gentler slope asks less effort of the people using the ramp, so the gentlest value stated by a current standard is the best practice found.

why_it_matters.text: Steeper ramps take more effort. Wheelchair users pushing up a {{slope=0.05241|3°}} slope used more force, torque and cadence than on the level (36 users with spinal cord injury).
The effort lands on the arms and shoulders. A 34-study review found slope effects under-studied.
People with multiple sclerosis spend more energy walking, and uphill feels harder than the measured cost suggests.
Going down matters too. At {{slope=1/12|1:12}} and {{slope=1/8|1:8}} most users coped, but power-chair users and people with vision impairment raised safety concerns on steeper descents.

Climbing a short ramp is not the same as managing it all day. In a 171-person trial only a few manual wheelchair users could not climb {{slope=1/8|1:8}} over {{len=9144|30 ft}}; it tested one ramp, not sustained use.
Codes set maximum slopes as gentle as {{slope=1/16.7|1:16.7}}, and several prefer {{slope=1/20|1:20}} or gentler. A legal limit is the least a code allows, not the best a design can do.

universal.basis: Best practice is what benefits the people it is for most. A gentler slope asks less effort of the people using the ramp, and {{slope=1/20|1:20}} is the gentlest value any current standard read states. No study or professional body in the library does better.
universal.short: Best practice based on standards in the UK, Ireland, France, Norway and ISO; no study in the library does better.

group.basis: Studies: a 36-person study of wheelchair users with spinal cord injury on level vs a {{slope=0.05241|3°}} slope (higher force uphill), a ramp slope/height/pushing-force study (abstract not retrieved), a 34-study review, and a 171-person trial in which most could climb {{slope=1/8|1:8}} over {{len=9144|30 ft}}. None derives a threshold.
group.short: Tier 3 studies show more force and effort on slopes but set no threshold; the value is taken from the standards.

group.who: People with spinal cord injury, especially higher lesions
group.statement: Not set. No SCI-specific threshold has been established.
group.basis: Gap GAP-019 is open. The one SCI slope study in the library enrolled users with lesions at T8-L2 (paraplegia); it does not cover the higher lesions (cervical) whose reduced arm function is the concern.

group.statement: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} or gentler, with places to rest
group.basis: This is the mechanism named in the item's title. Studies of people with multiple sclerosis show higher energy cost of walking and higher perceived uphill effort; they do not identify a slope threshold.
group.short: Uphill walking costs more effort; no study sets a threshold; the value and the rest places are inferred.

group.basis: The item lists chronic pain as an applicable group but the library holds no pain-specific evidence on ramp gradient (gap GAP-013 is recorded as closed).
A clinical-guideline update on upper-extremity preservation in spinal cord injury is in the library but is not linked to this item.

group.who: Ambulant people using a cane, crutches or walker
group.basis: The item's ramp specification assumes wheelchair use (gap GAP-014, recorded as closed). Studies of gait with a cane or walker on an incline exist but give no slope limit.

person.basis: No general value. The usable slope and length depend on the person's strength, stamina, equipment and the length of the route, so they are set by individual assessment (for example with an occupational therapist) and trial on the actual route. Design at this scale is individual by definition. Evidence on how much people differ: in the 171-person trial the range of tolerated slopes was wide.
person.short: An occupational therapist's assessment determines the position within the range, based on strength, stamina, equipment and route length.

evidence.relevance: Only SCI slope study in the library: 36 users, level vs {{slope=0.05241|3°}}, uphill raised force and cadence. Cannot set a threshold from one slope. The register names it as the '1:20 basis' - it is not a threshold derivation.

Systematic review (34 studies) of wheelchair biomechanics on slope, cross-slope, kerb and ground type. The source the gap register itself names for re-research. Not yet linked to this item's BPC; its duplicate record is REF-VERIFIED-003.
Ramp slope, ramp height and pushing force vs wheelchair-driving performance and muscle activity. Participant group not yet confirmed (abstract not retrieved). Duplicate record: REF-00030.
Normative walking energy cost for 260 healthy people. Background for energy arguments; not a disability or ramp study.
Threshold-crossing skill, 214 able-bodied learners in a manual wheelchair: a proxy population, and about thresholds rather than ramp slope.
Clinical-guideline update on upper-extremity preservation in spinal cord injury (consensus). Relevant to why effort on slopes matters; not linked to this item.

10 men with paraplegia pushing up {{slope=0.03492|2°}} to {{slope=0.2126|12°}} slopes: big changes in stroking and muscle activity between {{slope=0.06993|4°}} and {{slope=0.1763|10°}}. Describes effort, does not set a limit. Abstract-level read.

5 wheelchair users with cervical cord injury at 5% to 12.5% slopes: ability to climb differed widely between people (power 0.23, 0.24, 0.26 W/kg at 5%, 6.7%, 8.3%). Too small to set a threshold. Abstract-level read.

27 adults (manual and power wheelchair users, cane or service-animal users with vision impairment): {{slope=1/8|1:8}} and {{slope=1/12|1:12}} usable for most; {{slope=1/4|1:4}} unsafe; many manual users lacked the strength to climb unassisted. Small sample, no scooter or ambulation-aid users. Abstract-level read.
18 ambulant people with multiple sclerosis: uphill walking was the most demanding task and rated more demanding than energy cost suggests. Abstract-level read.
26 older adults using a cane or rolling walker on an incline: gait on the incline differed by device. Does not give a slope limit. Abstract-level read.
208 people with multiple sclerosis: 31% show walking-related motor fatigue in a 6-minute walk, up to about 51% at EDSS 6.5. Level-ground walking test, not a slope study. Abstract-level read.
7 able-bodied novices propelling a wheelchair at {{slope=0.06116|3.5°}}, {{slope=0.1673|9.5°}} and {{slope=0.2679|15°}}: peak pushrim force more than doubled. Healthy proxy, not wheelchair users.
24 healthy adults: {{slope=1/12|1:12}} and {{slope=1/10|1:10}} judged suitable; blood pressure higher at {{slope=1/6|1:6}}. Healthy proxy, not wheelchair users.

171 people with mobility impairments on {{slope=1/8|1:8}} to {{slope=1/20|1:20}} slopes over {{len=9144|30 ft}}: only a few manual wheelchair users could not ascend, even at {{slope=1/8|1:8}}; no change to the ADA slope or length recommended. Feasibility on one ramp, not repeated or sustained use. Counter-evidence to treating {{slope=1/20|1:20}} as a feasibility limit. Abstract-level read.
Meta-analysis of 9 studies: higher oxygen cost of walking in multiple sclerosis; weak association with fatigue. Supports the energy mechanism named in the item. Abstract-level read.

excluded_evidence_note: Of the 15 sources linked to this item's BPC, 11 do not concern ramps (6 on stairs; 5 on sit-to-stand, grab bars, luminance contrast, instrumented ADLs). REF-00387 is excluded because its stored title and DOI describe two different papers. Cross-slope studies found 2026-10-29 (REF-00743, REF-00744) are held back for the cross-slope item. REF-00748 (healthy gait on slopes) and REF-00749 (geared wheels) are in the library but not cited here.

jurisdictions.standard: Approved Document M, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings (England)
jurisdictions.headline: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} (going up to {{len=10000|10 m}}); {{slope=1/12|1:12}} at most, for goings up to {{len=2000|2 m}}
jurisdictions.note: A stepped route is also advised; alternative means of access when total rise is over {{len=2000|2 m}}
provisions: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} for a going up to {{len=10000|10 m}} (rise up to {{len=500|500 mm}}); {{slope=1/15|1:15}} up to {{len=5000|5 m}} (rise up to {{len=333|333 mm}}); {{slope=1/12|1:12}} up to {{len=2000|2 m}} (rise up to {{len=166|166 mm}}). Interpolate between: {{slope=1/14|1:14}} for a {{len=4000|4 m}} going, {{slope=1/19|1:19}} for {{len=9000|9 m}}.

No flight with a going over {{len=10000|10 m}} or a rise over {{len=500|500 mm}}. A lift or other alternative for wheelchair users when the total rise is over {{len=2000|2 m}}. Stated reason: a high rise is unacceptably tiring for wheelchair users and some people with walking difficulties, even with rest landings.

Gradients should be as shallow as practicable: steep gradients are hard for wheelchair users who lack the strength to climb or to slow down. Some ambulant disabled people find ramps harder than steps; people may need to stop frequently to regain strength or breath or ease pain.
Surface width between walls, upstands or kerbs at least {{len=1500|1.5 m}}; handrail on both sides (people with one-sided weakness need support on both).

Foot and head landing at least {{len=1200|1.2 m}} long, clear of door swings; intermediate landings at least {{len=1500|1.5 m}} long; passing places {{len=1800|1800 mm}} by {{len=1800|1800 mm}} where the far end is not visible or there are three flights or more. Landings level: no steeper than {{slope=1/60|1:60}} along their length, cross-fall no steeper than {{slope=1/40|1:40}}.

Kerb at least {{len=100|100 mm}} high on any open side, contrasting visually. Ramp surface slip-resistant when wet and in a colour that contrasts with the landings; similar friction on ramp and landings.
Clearly sign-posted steps are provided in addition when the rise of the ramp is over {{len=300|300 mm}} (two {{len=150|150 mm}} steps).
A section of an internal route with a gradient of {{slope=1/20|1:20}} or steeper is designed as a ramp to Table 1 and Diagram 3; level means no steeper than {{slope=1/60|1:60}}.
jurisdictions.vs_guidebook: The preferred gradient matches the Guidebook position ({{slope=1/20|1:20}}) but only for goings up to {{len=10000|10 m}}; {{slope=1/12|1:12}} is allowed for goings up to {{len=2000|2 m}}.

jurisdictions.clause: 1.1.3.4 Ramped access routes; Table 2; 2.1.3.4 existing buildings
jurisdictions.headline: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} preferred (up to {{len=10000|10 m}}); {{slope=1/12|1:12}} only for flights up to {{len=2000|2 m}}
jurisdictions.note: A stepped route must also be provided when the rise is more than {{len=300|300 mm}}
provisions: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} for a flight up to {{len=10000|10 m}} (rise up to {{len=500|500 mm}}); {{slope=1/15|1:15}} up to {{len=5000|5 m}} (rise up to {{len=333|333 mm}}); {{slope=1/12|1:12}} up to {{len=2000|2 m}} (rise up to {{len=166|166 mm}}). Interpolation is allowed between {{len=2000|2 m}} and {{len=10000|10 m}}.

Preferred maximum {{slope=1/20|1:20}}. Ramps not steeper than {{slope=1/12|1:12}} only where site constraints require it and each flight is no longer than {{len=2000|2000 mm}}. Stated reason: a person using or pushing a wheelchair may not have the strength to climb a steeper or longer flight, and there is a danger of falling forwards going down or backwards going up.

A gradient of {{slope=1/20|1:20}} or steeper is a ramp. A gradient steeper than {{slope=1/50|1:50}} but gentler than {{slope=1/20|1:20}} is a gently sloped route; {{slope=1/20|1:20}} or gentler is preferred.

Clear width between walls, upstands or kerbs at least {{len=1500|1500 mm}}; at least {{len=1200|1200 mm}} between handrails; handrails on both sides. A wide ramp is divided by extra handrails into channels {{len=1200|1200 mm}} to {{len=2500|2500 mm}} wide.

Level landing ({{slope=1/50|1:50}} or gentler counts as level) at top and bottom, at least {{len=1800|1800 mm}} long by {{len=1800|1800 mm}} wide and clear of door swings; intermediate landings at least {{len=1500|1500 mm}} long, and {{len=1800|1800 mm}} by {{len=1800|1800 mm}} as passing places where the far end of the ramp cannot be seen or there are three flights or more.
Upstand at least {{len=100|100 mm}} high on any open side of a ramp or landing, contrasting visually with the surface.

Where the rise is more than {{len=300|300 mm}}, a stepped route must be provided in addition to the ramp. Stated reason: some people find steps easier than a ramp, such as people with mobility difficulties who use certain walking aids, older people and people with vision impairment.

A platform lift or similar where the ramp is {{slope=1/20|1:20}} or steeper and the total rise is more than {{len=2000|2000 mm}}. Stated reason: ramps become too tiring for wheelchair users beyond that height.

Where the full figures are not practicable: {{slope=1/12|1:12}} flights up to {{len=4500|4500 mm}} (interpolating from {{slope=1/20|1:20}} at {{len=10000|10 m}}); width between handrails at least {{len=1000|1000 mm}}; top and bottom landings at least {{len=1500|1500 mm}} by {{len=1500|1500 mm}}; intermediate landings at least {{len=1000|1000 mm}} long.
jurisdictions.vs_guidebook: The preferred gradient matches the Guidebook position ({{slope=1/20|1:20}}). The {{slope=1/12|1:12}} maximum is confined to flights of {{len=2000|2 m}} or less.
